authorities: SEC v. Jarkesy, 603 U.S. 109 (2024)
Axon Enterprise, Inc. v. FTC, 598 U.S. 175 (2023)
FCC v. AT&T, Inc. (U.S. June 4, 2026) (FCC forfeiture orders upheld)
Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg, 492 U.S. 33 (1989)
kinds.label: Agency adjudication of penalties (jury trial / Article III)
kinds.lowers: Clarity falls to Arguable for settled or consented matters, FCC forfeiture orders (FCC v. AT&T) and cease-and-desist orders without money penalties; seriousness falls when no penalty wording is found.
kinds.raises: Clarity rises to Flagrant for SEC in-house civil penalties for fraud (Jarkesy).
kinds.why: The agency itself appears to be deciding a case that could carry penalties. Penalty cases resembling common-law suits may require a jury and an Article III court, and agency proceedings can combine prosecutor and judge in one body.

authorities: Lucia v. SEC, 585 U.S. 237 (2018)
United States v. Arthrex, Inc., 594 U.S. 1 (2021)
Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB, 561 U.S. 477 (2010)
kinds.label: Appointment of officers (ALJs, hearing officers, board members)
kinds.why: Officers who exercise significant federal power must be appointed in a manner the Appointments Clause allows, and their decisions must be reviewable by a principal officer.

authorities: Carter v. Carter Coal Co., 298 U.S. 238 (1936)
Department of Transportation v. Association of American Railroads, 575 U.S. 43 (2015)
Alpine Securities Corp. v. FINRA, 121 F.4th 1314 (D.C. Cir. 2024)
kinds.label: Government power exercised by a private corporation
kinds.lowers: Seriousness falls to Moderate for routine exchange and clearing-agency filings.
kinds.why: This action comes from a private, agency-supervised corporation. Delegating government power to private entities is limited by the private nondelegation doctrine and by Article II.

authorities: Alpine Securities Corp. v. FINRA, 121 F.4th 1314 (D.C. Cir. 2024)
kinds.label: Private corporation disciplining or expelling a member
kinds.why: A private, agency-supervised corporation appears to be imposing discipline. The D.C. Circuit has held that such a body may not expel a member without government review first.

authorities: West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022)
Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477 (2023)
FCC v. Consumers' Research, 606 U.S. ___ (2025)
kinds.label: Delegation and major questions
kinds.raises: Seriousness rises to Severe for rules designated significant or major.
kinds.why: Large or novel rules may exceed what Congress clearly authorized (major questions doctrine) or raise questions about how much lawmaking power Congress may hand to agencies (nondelegation).

authorities: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)
kinds.label: Agency interpretation of an ambiguous statute
kinds.raises: Clarity rises to Substantial when the document itself invokes Chevron-style deference.
kinds.why: Courts no longer defer to an agency's reading of an ambiguous statute; reliance on agency interpretation is a point to check.

authorities: Trump v. Slaughter (U.S. June 29, 2026)
Trump v. Cook (U.S. June 29, 2026)
Seila Law LLC v. CFPB, 591 U.S. 197 (2020)
Collins v. Yellen, 594 U.S. 220 (2021)
kinds.label: Presidential control and removal of agency leaders
kinds.why: In Trump v. Slaughter (2026) the Supreme Court overruled Humphrey's Executor and held that the President may remove FTC commissioners at will. Open questions remain about bodies the Court has treated differently, such as the Federal Reserve (Trump v. Cook, 2026), and about how far presidential direction of agency decisions may go.

authorities: Train v. City of New York, 420 U.S. 35 (1975)
CFPB v. Community Financial Services Ass'n, 601 U.S. 416 (2024)
Impoundment Control Act of 1974, 2 U.S.C. 681 et seq.
kinds.label: Spending, funding and appropriations
kinds.raises: Clarity and seriousness rise when appropriated money is withheld or rescinded.
kinds.why: Congress holds the power of the purse. Withholding, redirecting or self-funding money can raise Appropriations Clause and separation-of-powers questions.

authorities: Myers v. United States, 272 U.S. 52 (1926)
Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952)
kinds.label: Creating, abolishing or restructuring agencies and offices
kinds.raises: Clarity and seriousness rise when a statutory body is abolished or dismantled.
kinds.why: Agencies and offices are created by statute; executive changes to their structure or functions may raise separation-of-powers questions.

authorities: Murphy v. NCAA, 584 U.S. 453 (2018)
NFIB v. Sebelius, 567 U.S. 519 (2012)
Printz v. United States, 521 U.S. 898 (1997)
kinds.label: Federalism (states, preemption, conditions on federal funds)
kinds.raises: Clarity rises when state officials are directed to act (anti-commandeering).
kinds.why: Federal action that directs states, overrides state law, or attaches conditions to federal money can raise Tenth Amendment and Spending Clause questions.

authorities: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952)
Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (U.S. Feb. 20, 2026)
kinds.label: Executive action that may act like legislation
kinds.raises: Clarity rises to Flagrant for tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
kinds.why: Presidential orders must rest on the Constitution or a statute. Orders that impose duties, tariffs or suspend laws invite scrutiny of their legal basis.

authorities: Powell v. SEC, 149 F.4th 1029 (9th Cir. 2025)
SEC v. Romeril, 15 F.4th 166 (2d Cir. 2021)
Nebraska Press Ass'n v. Stuart, 427 U.S. 539 (1976)
kinds.label: Gag orders, no-deny terms and prior restraints on speech
kinds.raises: Clarity rises when the document describes a gag order or prior restraint.
kinds.why: Conditions that stop people from denying charges or discussing their case restrict speech. The SEC rescinded its no-deny rule in May 2026, but similar terms can appear in other agencies' settlements and orders.

authorities: Central Hudson Gas & Electric v. PSC, 447 U.S. 557 (1980)
Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel, 471 U.S. 626 (1985)
NRA v. Vullo, 602 U.S. 175 (2024)
kinds.label: Speech, press, religion or association
kinds.why: Rules about what people say, must disclose, publish or believe can raise First Amendment issues.

authorities: City of Los Angeles v. Patel, 576 U.S. 409 (2015)
Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. 296 (2018)
kinds.label: Searches, inspections, records demands or surveillance
kinds.why: Government inspections and demands for records or data can raise Fourth Amendment questions.

authorities: Cedar Point Nursery v. Hassid, 594 U.S. 139 (2021)
Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976)
Culley v. Marshall, 601 U.S. 377 (2024)
kinds.label: Property, takings or due process
kinds.raises: Clarity rises for action without notice or hearing; seriousness rises for loss of property or a license.
kinds.why: Taking property, revoking licenses or acting without notice and a hearing can raise Fifth Amendment due process or takings questions.

authorities: Timbs v. Indiana, 586 U.S. 146 (2019)
United States v. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. 321 (1998)
kinds.label: Excessive fines and forfeitures
kinds.raises: Triggered by penalties of a million dollars or more; seriousness rises for penalties in the billions.
kinds.why: Very large penalties and forfeitures can be tested against the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause, which asks whether a sanction is grossly disproportional to the offense.

authorities: Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, 600 U.S. 181 (2023)
kinds.label: Classifications by race, sex or other protected traits
kinds.raises: Clarity rises to Flagrant for express racial classifications or set-asides.
kinds.why: Government classifications by race or sex receive heightened scrutiny.

outcomes.label: Guidance, interpretation or request for comment
Decided or ordered after a contest

sanction_families.label: Exclusion from a market, profession or program

sanctions.label: FCC forfeitures and notices of apparent liability
Bars, bans and expulsions from an industry
Suspension from practising before an agency (accountants, lawyers)
Debarment and exclusion from government programs
Suspension of a license, registration or membership
Denial of an application, license or renewal
Orders to delete data, models or algorithms
Gag orders, no-deny and confidentiality terms, prior restraints
Seizure, forfeiture and condemnation of property
Warning letters, citations and notices of violation
Termination, suspension or conditioning of federal funds
Criminal charges, pleas, convictions and referrals

clarity.label: Clarity

levels.meaning: The action fits a pattern the Supreme Court has squarely held unlawful.
levels.name: Flagrant

levels.meaning: A strong argument under existing Supreme Court or federal appellate precedent.
levels.name: Substantial

levels.meaning: An open or developing question that deserves a lawyer's review. Not a lesser concern; a less settled one.
levels.name: Arguable

clarity.question: How clearly does existing law condemn this kind of action?

impact.label: Seriousness

levels.meaning: Penalties, bars, loss of livelihood or property, or economy-wide or presidential action.
levels.name: Severe

levels.meaning: Binding obligations on regulated parties or a whole industry.
levels.name: Significant

levels.meaning: Narrower, procedural or preliminary effects. Still a constitutional concern.
levels.name: Moderate

impact.question: How much is at stake if the action is unlawful?
